cim_eredeti: How To Approach Licensing and Budgeting for AI Education
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence is transforming the way higher education operates, but it’s also transforming the workforce students will enter once they graduate. AI literacy and other technology-related job skills are quickly becoming a requirement for employers across industries, and higher education institutions are responding by baking AI literacy into coursework.

Increasingly, many faculty are realizing that it’s no longer constructive to ban AI outright. Rather, students must understand the appropriate use cases for AI and must be able to document and explain their prompts and choices. Applying critical thinking to generative AI in education is a skill that employers are demanding and higher education institutions are working to instill in students.

As this trend grows, it’s raising an operational question for IT leaders: How do we fund and manage AI in the classroom?

Budgeting for AI tools in the classroom starts with determining exactly what you need. To do so, think about the goals. What should students be able to do with AI by the end of the course? What should they understand about how the tool functions? What demonstrable skills will they have learned? This can help determine the level of access they need, whether that’s basic chat, advanced analytics features or specialized computing resources. Those answers can also determine whether a course needs a consistent, university-provided tool or whether students can choose their own platforms.

Institutions that already use Microsoft or Google products likely have access to some of their AI features, but the capabilities and level of access depends on the institution’s licensing agreement. A shared platform could make it easier for instructors to deliver a consistent learning experience and would give the IT team greater control over the security posture of the tool.

Students also might arrive to class with their own subscriptions to AI platforms, which offers them a greater level of flexibility. However, these tools can be harder for institutions to manage. Security guardrails and clear policies can mitigate the risks these tools bring, but they’re not foolproof, so detailed guidance and training are vital to ensure students understand what data they can and cannot feed into their personal tools.

EXPLORE: Institutions lean on existing investments when launching AI tools.

For institutions seeking the standardized approach, first look at existing agreements with vendors to see what features are already included before purchasing additional access.

It’s also important to distinguish usage from licensing in AI pricing models. Basic chat functionality typically falls under a basic license or covered under defined usage parameters. But more resource-intensive activities, such as analyzing data sets or using different models, consume more tokens and can lead to higher costs.

Of course, every student and class have different needs, which is why the upfront analysis of goals and outcomes is necessary to determine how to budget for AI usage. Also, courses are different lengths, while licenses are typically annual, so consider whether a yearlong license is worth it for a student taking a class that only lasts a few months.

There are a few ways to pay for these tools. Because these skills are increasingly seen as imperative for workforce development, some state and federal workforce programs may help institutions cover the costs of AI for students. Some institutions recover costs through course or technology fees, though this can affect enrollment. Others have placed resource-intensive AI tools in a lab environment. This ensures the hardware can support the platforms and reduces the per-student licensing costs.

The AI landscape is constantly shifting, which can make planning for long-term academic adoption of the tools complex. Grant funding opportunities may not exist year to year, leaving institutions to pick up the tab after the initial awards. Students may be reluctant to enroll in courses that are adding to their already costly tuition.

There are a few steps institutions can take to ensure they’re set up to support a sustainable AI curriculum.

Reviewing the academic goals and outcomes as an institutional priority can earn buy-in from university leadership. Connecting the proposed investments to overall institutional goals helps build a case for ongoing budget prioritization.

Usage forecasting can be helpful in predicting future costs, but actual demand can be unclear, as a small number of users might account for a large share of activity, particularly when advanced features are available. Institutions should plan to monitor usage and adjust access or budgets as they learn what students and faculty need.

Training and adoption are also key elements of a long-term, cost-effective AI strategy. A license does not ensure that a tool will be used effectively. Faculty and students need support, and institutions need a way to assess whether the investment is helping meet goals. A pilot can reveal real usage patterns, unexpected costs and support needs before a program expands.

There is no single licensing or funding model that will fit every institution. CDW can work with higher education institutions to shape an AI adoption plan around their workforce development goals. Working together, we can identify the programs and students who would benefit most, and match AI tools and licensing to course needs. Our experts can help institutions explore potential funding opportunities and think through how to sustain long-term access, giving institutions a clearer picture of the costs involved beyond an initial pilot or funding cycle.

By setting clear goals and planning for access, security, training and funding, institutions can make AI a practical part of workforce development education.
